content.title: About
content.content: Pistachio nuts are the edible seeds of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera), native to the Mediterranean, Iran, the United States and other warm regions. Raw pistachios have a mildly sweet, buttery flavor and a crunchy texture. They are eaten in the shell, used in cooking, confectionery, pastes and ice cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pistachios belong to the Anacardiaceae family and are more closely related to cashews than to almonds.
About 70 % of pistachios naturally split open at maturity, making harvest easier.
The shell only opens naturally on ripe nuts; immature nuts stay closed.
Pistachios are often called “green gold” because of their bright color and high nutritional value.
In Iran pistachios have been cultivated for over 3,000 years and are a national symbol.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis, aiding brain function.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in pistachios is monounsaturated, which can help maintain cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Pistachios provide lutein, zeaxanthin and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High in plant protein and fiber
items.content: One cup of raw pistachios delivers about 20 g of protein and 10 g of dietary fiber, promoting satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support normal muscle function.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Pistachios can trigger allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Raw pistachios are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Whole pistachios may pose a choking risk for young children; finely chopped nuts are safer.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Pistachios contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in prone individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pistachios can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, cereals, baked goods, sauces and pastes. They are common in Middle‑Eastern dishes, ice cream and desserts. Before eating you may lightly roast or dry‑toast them without added salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pistachios in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid or stale.
